document_check.note: The document is Wischik CM et al. 'Clinical, imaging and blood biomarker outcomes in a Phase 3 clinical trial of tau aggregation inhibitor hydromethylthionine mesylate in mild cognitive impairment and mild to moderate dementia due to Alzheimer's disease', J Prev Alz Dis 13 (2026) 100480 (TRx-237-039, NCT03446001). It is a randomised disease-modifying therapy trial that reports safety and efficacy outcomes, as the cited context describes.

cited_result: The review cites the trial's safety and efficacy outcomes in general. The appraised principal result is the prespecified co-primary efficacy comparison at 52 weeks: change in ADAS-cog11 and ADCS-ADL23, HMTM 16 mg/day vs MTC 4 mg twice weekly, ITT n=598 (difference -0.42, p=0.5601, and 0.36, p=0.7431).
tool_reason: The cited result is a randomised comparison of interventions from a trial, so RoB 2 applies, assessing the effect of assignment.

domains.rationale: This is a randomised (4:1:4), regulated multicentre phase 3 trial, so the sequence was probably random. The main text defers methods to the Supplementary and does not describe allocation concealment. Baseline characteristics in Table 1 are balanced on age, sex, MMSE and diagnosis. The APOE e4 difference (55.1% control vs 45.8% HMTM 16 mg) is compatible with chance.

signalling.question: 1.1 Was the allocation sequence random?
signalling.quote: Eligible participants were randomised at baseline in a 4:1:4 ratio to receive HMTM 16 mg/day (administered as two 4 mg tablets twice daily), 8 mg/day (administered as one 4 mg tablet and one blank tablet containing only excipients twice daily), or excipient-only tablets given twice daily among which were included 4 mg MTC tablets given every 2–4 days (4 mg twice weekly).

signalling.question: 1.2 Was the allocation sequence concealed until participants were enrolled and assigned to interventions?
signalling.quote: Searched Methods 2.3 and 2.4 for central or interactive web or voice randomisation, numbered identical drug packs, or any concealment method; the main text states 'Details of sample size determination and statistical methods are provided in the Supplementary.'

signalling.question: 1.3 Did baseline differences between intervention groups suggest a problem with the randomisation process?

domains.domain: D2 Deviations from intended interventions (effect of assignment)
domains.rationale: The 52-week phase was double-blind, with a low-dose MTC urinary colourant control and excipient tablets used to keep the blind. The authors admit discolouration 'hampers maintenance of the blind', but the control was designed to mimic it. The primary efficacy analysis used the ITT population of 598. That the control arm had pharmacological activity is a feature of the chosen comparator, not a deviation from the intended intervention (see applicability).

signalling.question: 2.1 Were participants aware of their assigned intervention during the trial?
signalling.quote: In brief, TRx-237–039 compared HMTM as monotherapy at doses 16 mg/day and 8 mg/day with MTC 4 mg twice weekly on a varying schedule as control to ensure blinding.

signalling.question: 2.2 Were carers and people delivering the interventions aware of participants' assigned intervention during the trial?
signalling.quote: The initial 52-week blinded period was followed by a 52-week modified delayed start open label period in which all participants received 16 mg/day.

signalling.question: 2.3 to 2.5 Deviations arising because of the trial context
signalling.quote: Not applicable: these questions are asked only if 2.1 or 2.2 is Yes, Probably yes or No information.

signalling.question: 2.6 Was an appropriate analysis used to estimate the effect of assignment to intervention?
signalling.quote: The 598 patients in the primary efficacy analysis had a mean age of 72 years.

domains.rationale: Only 79% completed to 52 weeks, and the main text reports no analysis showing robustness to missing data. In dementia trials, withdrawal can depend on decline; the authors themselves describe biased withdrawal in an earlier MTC trial. Completion was similar across arms (76% to 81%), which makes it less likely that missingness depended on the true outcome.

signalling.question: 3.1 Were data for this outcome available for all, or nearly all, participants randomised?
signalling.quote: of whom 470 (79 %) completed the study to 52 weeks (Fig. 1).

signalling.question: 3.2 Is there evidence that the result was not biased by missing outcome data?
signalling.quote: Searched Methods and Results for multiple imputation, tipping-point or other missing-data sensitivity analyses of the co-primary endpoints; statistical methods are deferred to the Supplementary.

signalling.question: 3.3 Could missingness in the outcome depend on its true value?
signalling.quote: A true placebo was used in the first dose-finding Phase 2 study with MTC, but there was biased withdrawal in the placebo arm, particularly of participants with more rapid clinical decline, resulting in reduced overall decline [19].

signalling.question: 3.4 Is it likely that missingness in the outcome depended on its true value?
signalling.quote: Study completion was high (79 %), with no difference between the three treatment groups (76 % to 81 %).

domains.rationale: ADAS-cog and ADCS-ADL are standard instruments, given on the same visit schedule in every arm. Efficacy raters were separate from the assessor who handled eligibility and safety, and the phase was double-blind.

signalling.question: 4.1 Was the method of measuring the outcome inappropriate?
signalling.quote: The co-primary endpoints were comparison of change over 52 weeks in the 11-item Alzheimer's Disease Assessment Scale-Cognitive Subscale (ADAS-Cog11, determined from the administered 13-item ADAS-cog13 version)

signalling.question: 4.2 Could measurement or ascertainment of the outcome have differed between intervention groups?
signalling.quote: Five post-baseline visits were scheduled during the double-blind treatment phase (Supplementary).

signalling.question: 4.3 Were outcome assessors aware of the intervention received by study participants?
signalling.quote: Eligibility and safety assessments were performed by an independent qualified medical assessor not involved in efficacy assessments.

signalling.question: 4.4 and 4.5 Influence of knowledge of intervention on assessment
signalling.quote: Not applicable: asked only if 4.3 is Yes, Probably yes or No information.

domains.domain: D5 Selection of the reported result
domains.rationale: The trial was registered and its design published beforehand. The co-primary endpoints are those prespecified, and the null prespecified result is reported in full, so selective reporting of this result is unlikely.

signalling.question: 5.1 Were the data analysed in accordance with a pre-specified analysis plan that was finalised before unblinded outcome data were available?
signalling.quote: The design and rationale for the trial have been described in this journal previously [4].

signalling.question: 5.2 Is the numerical result likely to have been selected from multiple eligible outcome measurements?
signalling.quote: ADAS-Cog11, determined from the administered 13-item ADAS-cog13 version

signalling.question: 5.3 Is the numerical result likely to have been selected from multiple eligible analyses of the data?
signalling.quote: None of the comparisons of HMTM 16 mg/day was significantly different from MTC 4 mg twice weekly for the co-primary outcomes.

applicability.rationale: The control was MTC 4 mg twice weekly, not an inert placebo, and the authors conclude that it was pharmacologically active: 'We now report that even this very low dose had clinical therapeutic activity over 52 weeks' (p6). The randomised contrast is HMTM against an active low dose.
Participants were amyloid-PET-positive, with MMSE 16 to 27. Only 44% (263/598) had MCI; the rest had mild to moderate AD dementia. So the whole-population co-primary result is only partly about MCI.

'The study was financed entirely by TauRx Therapeutics Ltd. TauRx took the lead in study design and conduct, data interpretation, and report preparation.' (p3). This is not a RoB 2 domain but is relevant to interpretation.

overall_rationale: Domains 2, 4 and 5 are low risk. Domain 1 has some concerns because allocation concealment is not described in the main text. Domain 3 has some concerns because 21% did not complete to 52 weeks and no missing-data sensitivity analysis is shown, although completion was balanced. Two domains have some concerns, but in a blinded, registered, regulated phase 3 trial with balanced withdrawal these concerns do not substantially lower confidence. So the overall judgment is some concerns, not high.
